Thomas Tallis. The greatest English composer of the Tudor period, who lived around 1505 to 1585 and was a versatile master equally skilled in Catholic Latin motets and Protestant English anthems. He navigated the treacherous religious shifts of his era with uncompromising artistry.

Tallis composed the forty-voice motet Spem in Deum, also sometimes titled the Tallis Motets. This was an extraordinary feat of polyphonic density and tonal balance that stands among the most complex vocal works of the Renaissance. He created an extensive English service repertoire, setting the Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer, and in doing so defined the Anglican choral tradition. He served at the Chapel Royal in London for nearly forty years, surviving religious upheavals under Henry the Eighth, Edward the Sixth, Mary the First, and Elizabeth the First by being artistically indispensable.

Tallis was a master of modal counterpoint with an instinctive sense of harmonic color and cadential clarity that was unusual for his era. His Latin motets, including works on penitential and Marian texts, suggest his private Catholic conviction, while his English anthems served the established church with equal skill. He composed for all available vocal combinations, from simple three-voice works to massive polyphonic canvases, and each was always singable with clarity. His seamless vocal writing and harmonic sophistication established the foundation for English cathedral music that would follow.
